_note: Carriers other than seagoing hulls and animals (those are in 99_ships.json and 90_additions.json): the vehicles and rigs that carriage wears out (Complaints/629). Every mass, hour count and allocation is an estimate marked in each yield_basis. carrier_use.serves names which geography mode carrier input the good supplies; days_per_year is the days a unit works in a year.

cart.basis: per two-wheeled cart without its team or harness
cart.yield_basis: MASS: geography's CART_SELF_MASS_KG (sim/geography/transport.py), 200 kg empty, cited there as 150-250 kg for a two-wheeled wood-and-iron cart; allocated here as 0.25 m3 of retained timber at the timber recipe density of 600 kg/m3 (150 kg) plus about 15 kg of iron tyre strips, nails and axle fittings; 0.4 m3 is bought to allow shaping offcuts. LABOUR: 150 carpenter hours (wheel making is most of it) and 15 smith hours are TEMPORARY HEURISTICS, confidence D, no source found, not a measured work log. No price sets the bill. Retire when a measured wheelwright's work log is found (complaint 629 follow-up). NAILS: 3 of the 15 kg of iron are nails and small fittings (nails_kg) and 12 kg is bar, the split is a LABELLED HEURISTIC, conf D, no source found; retire: Complaints/533. SOURCE READ (Pass 8): Colonial Williamsburg wheelwright John Boag (podcast.history.org, 'Carriages, Carts and Wagons', https://podcast.history.org/2007/09/03/carriages-carts-and-wagons/, opened): a coach wheel takes about 100 hours of production, a wheelbarrow wheel 12, and a wagon took three workers five months. Two cart wheels at 50 to 100 hours each is 100 to 200 hours before the body and axle, which brackets the 150 carpenter hours only loosely; left at 150 (no work log of a plain cart found). Conf D. Pass 12: Merchant and Makers, 'Wheelwrighting, Mike Rowland and Son' (https://www.merchantandmakers.com/wheelwrighting-mike-rowland-and-son/, opened): 'A wheel could take a whole day to make, and that's working flat out', so a modern wheelwright makes two wheels in about 20 hours, a fifth of the 100 hours Boag's shop implies; the page gives no time for a whole cart. The 150 hours sit between 20 and 200 hours for the wheels alone plus the body and axle; no cart work log found.

pack_saddle.basis: per wood-framed pack saddle with girth and breeching rigging, for one animal
pack_saddle.yield_basis: MASS: geography's PACK_SADDLE_MASS_KG, 15 kg for a loaded rig before cargo (10-20 kg cited there). Allocated as a wooden frame of about 0.01 m3 (6 kg at 600 kg/m3; 0.02 m3 bought), 6 kg of leather and 2 kg of cord for girths and padding. LABOUR: 40 leatherworker (saddler) and 10 carpenter hours are TEMPORARY HEURISTICS, confidence D, author's estimates. Retire with a measured saddler's work log (complaint 629 follow-up). Pass 12 searched for a pack saddle build time: only a commercial page giving 120 to 150 hours for a full riding saddle (diy.alibaba.com, seen in a search result, not opened) and forum threads (leatherworker.net) on sawbuck trees with no hours; nothing opened bounds the 40 and 10 hours.

river_barge.basis: per flat-bottomed river or canal barge towed from a path, without cargo or team
river_barge.yield_basis: MASS: geography's BARGE_SELF_MASS_KG (sim/geography/transport.py), 3000 kg empty (a few tonnes, confidence D there). Allocated as 4.5 m3 of retained timber at 600 kg/m3 (about 2700 kg) plus 30 kg iron fastenings, 40 kg tar and 20 kg cord; 5 m3 is bought for offcuts. LABOUR: about a sixth of the merchant ship's shipwright hours, with a helper share like the ship's; TEMPORARY HEURISTICS, confidence D. Retire with measured barge scantlings and build logs (complaint 629 follow-up). Pass 12: no build log of a flat-bottomed barge found. The nearest opened source, the Sea Stallion replica (27,000 man hours for a 30 m, 150 cubic metre ship, https://www.vikingeskibsmuseet.dk/en/professions/boatyard/experimental-archaeological-research/ship-reconstruction/skuldelev-2, opened) scaled as in merchant_ship (hours with length squared, wood with length cubed) to a barge of about 12 m (ASSUMED; the Yahoo News piece on the Seneca Chief, https://www.yahoo.com/news/back-future-erie-canal-boat-112000527.html, opened, says the Erie canal boat it copies was 73 feet long and weighed 40 tons, without build hours) gives 27,000 * (12 / 30)^2 = 4,300 hours and 150 * (12 / 30)^3 = 9.6 cubic metres of wood, 7x the 600 hours and 2x the 5 cubic metres here: the hours are more than 3x low for a sea-going hull and no flat-bottomed build was found to say a plain barge is cheaper, so the figures are kept as a lower bound and left D.
